# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries,
diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be
ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you
plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.

To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA
lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each
folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look, a REQUIREMENTS.md
describing how the PWA works and a TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md describing how it is built.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how this is built, and
[TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how it is checked.

## One app, one setup

Mine installs as **one** app on the phone, with one icon. The apps in the subfolders are pages
inside it, not separate installs.

This is what makes the central requirement work: **the GitHub repo and token are entered once,
in the main app, and every app in a subfolder uses them.** Verified on iPhone and Android.

## Main app

A tile per app: its `icon.svg` above its folder name.

Above the tiles, apps may contribute a summary. The calendar's shows today's entries and the
next one — which matters, because opening the app is the only reminder that works (see below).

## First run

1. Open the app URL and add it to the home screen (iOS: Share → Add to Home Screen;
   Android: menu → Install).
2. The setup screen asks for GitHub owner, data repo, branch, and a personal access token.
3. The app tests the connection and reports clearly if it fails.

Settings are stored on the device only. The token is never displayed again after entry, and the
app warns 14 days before it expires.

Two settings belong to Mine rather than to any one app, and the same two rows appear in the main
settings and in each app's: **theme** (system, light or dark) and **date format** (auto, which
follows the device's locale, or `dd.mm.yyyy`, or `mm/dd/yy`). Both default to following the
device, so Mine looks like the rest of the phone until you say otherwise.

One convention is the same in every app: **a save icon is green and a trashcan is red**, wherever
either appears — a trashcan is red even where it only clears one field of one entry, because the
rule is the icon, not the consequence. Both are **glyphs on no
background**: a save is a green disk, a trashcan is a red trashcan. **Nothing in Mine is a filled
green button.** The weight of a primary action comes from the icon being the familiar one in the
familiar place, not from a block of colour — and a save drawn like the rest of the row cannot be
mistaken for a background that means something. The `x` that closes or abandons something is
neither green nor red, and stays plain.

A second convention follows from it: **the `x` is rightmost in every popup**, and the row ends
trashcan, save, `x`. The way out of an overlay is in the same corner wherever you are, so leaving
one is never something to look for — and that corner is worth more to the button reached for by
habit than to the one aimed at deliberately. The save keeps its familiar place beside it, which
is enough, because what makes it findable is the green disk and not the edge of the card.

## Markdown bodies

Every app keeps its text as markdown, so every app has to show it. **One renderer, in `shared/`,
used by all of them** — the calendar's details body today, a zettelkasten note and a diary entry
next. Two renderers would drift, and a note that looked right in one app and wrong in the next
would be the plainest possible sign that these files are not as portable as the whole idea claims.

It is **deliberately small**, and covers what a personal note actually holds: paragraphs, `#` to
`###` headings, bullet and numbered lists, `- [ ]` and `- [x]` checkboxes, **bold**, *italic*,
`code`, and links. No tables, no blockquotes, no fenced code blocks and no images — each of them
is more code to own for something an agenda or a diary page rarely carries, and the app that first
genuinely needs one can add it then.

A checkbox is **rendered, not operated**: `- [x]` draws a ticked box, and ticking it is an edit of
the text like any other. A body is read far more often than its checklist is advanced, and a
tappable box would have to write a file from a screen whose whole point is that it writes nothing.

**It builds nodes, never HTML.** The renderer makes DOM elements and sets text, so nothing in a
body can turn into markup: a body carrying a `<script>` tag shows that tag as text. This is the
threat the CSP exists for — injected script on our own origin — and a data file in your own repo
is the likeliest thing to carry a stray angle bracket. A link is rendered only for `http`, `https`
and `mailto`; anything else stays text, so a `javascript:` URL is never something to press. Links
open in a new tab, because leaving the app would lose the view you were in.

It is hand-written rather than vendored. It is small enough to be, and the dependency table in
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) asks of everything in it what would be
wrong with hand-rolling it — for this, nothing.

## Using it

- Changes appear instantly and are queued for GitHub in the background.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error. It is also a button: pressing it opens the
  calendar's `logs`, which says what the last attempt did and what is still waiting.
- Offline, the queue is kept and sent when you are back online or reopen the app. **Every open
  and every window focus retries it**, whatever went wrong last time, because a queue nothing
  retries is a queue that never empties — a browser left reporting a count it can neither
  explain nor clear.
- Editing the same entry on two devices never loses either version: the other device's version
  keeps the file, yours is kept beside it and flagged, and the sync indicator tells you there is
  something to review. Nothing is discarded and nothing is silently overwritten — but the app
  does not interrupt you to ask which to keep, because by then you are somewhere else.
- Everything works offline, including dates and search, because the app keeps a full local copy.

## Reminders

**Mine cannot notify you while it is closed.** No browser can schedule a notification for later;
this is a platform limitation, not a missing feature. Alerts are stored with each entry and
exported, and they fire while the app is open. The summary on the tile screen is the reminder.

## Updates

When a new version is deployed the app shows "Update ready — reload". It never updates while you
are in the middle of editing.

The banner appears only when the version waiting to take over genuinely differs from the one
running. A new worker can sit waiting while being identical to the active one, so "a worker is
waiting" is not the test — if it were, the banner would appear on an app with no update at all
and never go away. Reloading twice with no deploy in between must leave no banner.

## Privacy

Your data lives in a **private** repo. The app itself is public, but it contains no data, and the
token is scoped so that it can only touch the data repo.

# Mine — technical requirements

How [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) is built. Everything here was verified against the live
API or on device on 2026-11-19; `spike/` re-runs the device checks and needs no token.

## Repos

| Repo | Visibility | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maximilianharr/mine` | public | this app, served by Pages at `/mine/` |
| `maximilianharr/mine-data` | **private** | the markdown data |

Pages cannot serve a private repo without Enterprise, so data in the app repo would be
world-readable at a predictable URL. The token is scoped to the data repo only.

## Layout

One `manifest.json` with `scope: /mine/`, one service worker at the root. Subfolders are ordinary
pages inside that scope. `/mine/` and `/mine/calendar/` are the same origin, so they share one
IndexedDB — that is the whole mechanism behind "enter the token once".

```
/index.html /manifest.json /sw.js
/shared/  apps.js  store.js  github.js  md.js  markdown.js  prefs.js  vendor/
/calendar/  index.html  app.js  data.js  ui.js  views.js  kanban.js  popup.js  settings.js
            style.css  icon.svg  sample/
/test/    run.sh  unit.mjs  serve.py  check.mjs
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no node_modules. `git push` deploys, every page opens from
disk, all paths relative so the `/mine/` prefix needs no config.

The checks in `test/` hold to the same rule: `run.sh` drives a headless Chromium over the
DevTools protocol with nothing installed, and what it covers — and the two mistakes that make
it lie to you — are in [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md).

`shared/apps.js` exports the app list and is imported by both the tile screen and `sw.js`, so
adding an app means editing one array, and its `files` are what the worker precaches. The list is
written by hand on purpose: `install` uses `cache.addAll`, which rejects as a whole if any URL
404s, so a wrong entry fails loudly at install. A *missing* one fails silently, which is how
`shared/markdown.js` stayed out of the shell while `popup.js` imported it — an app installed and
taken offline before an entry was ever opened could not draw a details body.

`shared/md.js` and `shared/markdown.js` are two different jobs and stay two files. `md.js` is the
file envelope — it parses and serialises frontmatter and is imported by the paths that read and
write the repo. `markdown.js` renders a body for the screen and is imported only by UI, so nothing
on the file-IO path pulls a renderer in. It **returns a DOM node and never a string of HTML**, which
is what makes a body carrying a `<script>` tag harmless without a sanitiser to get right; what it
covers and why it is hand-rolled rather than vendored is in
[REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies).

## Fetching the repo

There is one read path, `pull`, and it is also the first mirror: with no stored ETag it fetches
the tree and every blob in it. A GraphQL query returning a folder's contents and blob SHAs in a
single request was built and measured — cost 1, 145 files in 6 s — and then never wired in,
because `pull` already handled the first run and the empty repo. It was deleted rather than left
as a second way to do the same thing; against a mirror measured in single-digit MB, fetched once
per device, the request count it saved was not worth a path nothing exercised.

**Do not use the tarball.** `GET /tarball/{ref}` 302-redirects to `codeload.github.com`, which
answers `access-control-allow-origin: https://render.githubusercontent.com` — one specific
foreign origin. `fetch()` applies CORS to the final response after the redirect, so it is
blocked, and the preflight an authenticated request needs returns 403. `api.github.com/graphql`
by contrast sends `allow-origin: *` and a 204 preflight allowing `Authorization`.

**A repo with no commits rejects the Git Data API outright.** Not just the ref read — `POST
/git/blobs` itself answers 409 "Git Repository is empty", so there is nothing to build a tree
from. Only `PUT /contents/{path}` can create the first commit. The first queued file goes that
way, and everything after drains normally once a history exists.

## Pull

1. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits/{branch}` with `If-None-Match`. A 304 means nothing changed and
   costs no rate-limit quota, and no ETag at all means a first mirror.
2. On 200: fetch the tree, diff blob SHAs, fetch only changed files, drop deleted paths.

Run on app open and on window focus. Background Sync does not exist in Safari, so all syncing is
foreground.

**A queue is drained first and the pull waits for it**, and the pull runs only if the drain got
through: whatever fails a drain — the token, the network — fails a pull too, and pulling over a
dirty queue rewrites the mirror underneath the changes still in it.

## Writes — one commit per drain

Queue each change locally with the blob SHA it was based on, then drain the whole queue as one
commit via the Git Data API: `POST /git/blobs` per file, `POST /git/trees` with `base_tree`
(deletion = entry with `sha: null`), `POST /git/commits`, `PATCH /git/refs/heads/{branch}` with
the expected old SHA and **no force**.

One drain is one commit, so a move — delete plus create, because the date is in the path and the
API has no rename — cannot be half-applied, and a 20-item offline backlog is one commit.

**A drain removes the keys it read, never the store.** `queued()` returns each item with its key,
and the drain deletes exactly those keys when the commit lands. Clearing the store instead would
discard anything queued *while the drain was in flight* — a save made during a slow push — and
that loss is silent and total: the item's text stays in the mirror under the blob SHA it was
based on, and the next pull deletes the file for not being in the remote. The next drain picks up
those later keys. For the same reason the first commit into an empty repo now takes only its own
item out of the queue and leaves the rest where they are, rather than clearing and re-adding
them, which also keeps their queued-at times.

A rejected ref update means someone pushed elsewhere: pull, rebuild on the new base, retry. This
succeeds, because nearly every write is a create at a freshly generated path.

**True conflict** = a queued change whose base SHA no longer matches the remote blob **and whose
text differs from it**. Remote keeps the canonical path; the local version is committed beside it
as `<name>.conflict-<yyyymmdd>.md` with `conflictOf:`. Nothing is discarded and the queue never
jams.

**One tree entry per path, and no impossible deletion.** The queue is collapsed to the last
queued op per path before the tree is built, and a queued delete whose path is not in the remote
listing is dropped. `sha: null` on a path that `base_tree` does not contain answers **422
`GitRPC::BadObjectState`** and refuses the whole commit — and it refuses it identically on every
retry, so one such item wedges the queue for good. A file moved or deleted before the queue ever
drained is exactly that case, because a move is a delete of a path GitHub never saw: with the
date in the path, changing an unpushed entry's date queues `del <old>` for a path that was only
ever local. Dropping it is also what was asked for — the file is gone locally and GitHub has
nothing to remove. If every queued item turns out to be such a no-op, the queue is cleared and
no commit is made.

This is also why a concurrent delete from another device heals itself: the listing is re-read on
every attempt, so the path is gone from it and the entry is dropped rather than refused.

**A matching text is a receipt, not a conflict.** A drain that died between the ref update and
the queue being cleared leaves items behind whose base SHA no longer matches — because the remote
now holds our own commit. Those are dropped, not forked: the blob is fetched in that branch
anyway, so comparing it costs no request, and without the comparison the app forks its own
committed work into `.conflict` files on the next attempt.

**Every attempt is retried.** The queue is never a reason to skip a drain, including on 401/403:
the error is reported and recorded, and the next open or focus tries again. The user needs one
thing from a failure, which is to be told what it was.

## The sync record

One row in `kv` under `sync.last`, written inside `drain()` and `pull()` so that every caller is
covered — both apps' refreshes, the calendar's background push — and so the reason outlives the
status line, which the next focus overwrites.

`{ at, lastAt, count, app, op, outcome, status, detail }`. A repeat of the same op, outcome and
status bumps `count` and `lastAt` rather than appending, because a wedged queue is retried on
every window focus and twenty copies of one 403 would bury the pull that explains it. A 304 pull
is not an attempt at anything and is not recorded. It is one row and not a history: what is worth
knowing is what is failing and for how long.

Queued items carry `at`, the time they were queued, so a backlog can be told from a jam.

**Discarding the queue repairs the mirror.** `discardQueue()` clears it, forgets the local copy
of every path it held, and drops the ETag — the next pull then restores exactly what GitHub
holds. Forgetting the queue alone would leave unpushable text in the mirror filed under the blob
SHA it was based on, which every later pull would compare as equal and skip forever.

## Service worker

Registered `{type: 'module'}` so it can import `shared/apps.js`. A version constant names the
cache; install precaches the shell. Same-origin requests are cache-then-revalidate.

Requests to `api.github.com` **bypass the worker entirely** — caching an API response would hand
back a stale ETag and silently break sync.

A new worker waits; the UI offers "Update ready — reload" and `skipWaiting()` runs only on tap.

**The offer is gated on the version, not on a worker waiting.** The worker answers a `version`
message over a `MessageChannel` port with its `VERSION` constant, and the page compares the
waiting worker's answer with the active one's; equal answers mean no banner. A worker that is
byte-identical to the running one can sit in `waiting` indefinitely, and `reg.waiting` alone as
the condition is what makes the banner appear on an app with no update and never go away. A
worker too old to answer reports `null` after a 1.5 s timeout, which differs from a real version
and so still offers the update.

## Token and CSP

Stored plaintext in IndexedDB with its expiry: as safe as the unlocked device. The threat that
matters is injected script on our own origin, closed off by policy rather than encryption:

```
default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.github.com
```

**No CDNs, ever.** Dependencies are committed to `/shared/vendor/`, pinned by hand, with source
URL and version in `VENDOR.md`. The token is never written to a log, a URL, or the DOM.

The OAuth device flow is not an option: GitHub's `login/device/code` endpoints send no CORS
headers, so a fine-grained PAT is the only no-backend path.

## Dependencies

| What | Why not hand-rolled |
| --- | --- |
| `js-yaml` | Files are hand-edited and must parse as real YAML — quoting, multiline scalars, flow maps. A subset parser misreads them silently. |
| `rrule` | `FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR` and DST-crossing weeklies are where hand-rolled expansion is wrong without telling you. |

YAML *writing* is ours (~20 lines): we control the output shape, so no dumper is needed.

**Load with `CORE_SCHEMA`, never js-yaml's default.** The default is YAML 1.1 and parses
`start: 2026-04-18` into a JS Date at UTC midnight — silently shifting every all-day entry by a
day east of UTC. `CORE_SCHEMA` keeps it a string and still handles bools, numbers, flow maps and
quoted scalars. This is the same off-by-one the bare-date format exists to prevent, arriving
through the parser instead.

## Platform findings

Verified in both installed home-screen apps (iPhone/Safari, Pixel/Chrome) on 2026-11-19.

| | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Storage shared across paths | **Yes.** A marker written by `/mine/spike/` was read back byte-identical by `/mine/spike/sub/`, both reporting `STANDALONE`. Cross-path module imports work too. |
| `{type:'module'}` service worker | Registers on Safari as well as Chrome. No classic fallback needed. |
| `storage.persisted()` | **Already granted**, no prompt, on both. An installed app is exempt from the ~7-day eviction that applies to uninstalled sites, so the token and mirror survive idle periods. |
| Quota | 35 GB (iPhone), 56 GB (Pixel), against a mirror measured in single-digit MB. |

Not tested, and no longer relevant: whether separately-installed PWAs get isolated storage. That
expectation is why the one-app topology was chosen.

Re-run `spike/` after a major iOS release — two of the four results above contradicted the
documented platform behaviour, and that is exactly the kind of thing that regresses silently.

content.text:
I read the whole repo (root app, `shared/`, `calendar/`, `sw.js`, both stylesheets, the test harness, all three docs). Here's what I found.

## Assumptions

- A new app is diary-shaped: its own folder, frontmatter + markdown bodies, pushes through the shared queue, has a settings panel and some overlays.
- The constraints stay: no build step, one install, one service worker, one IndexedDB, folder-per-app.

## What is already right — don't touch it

The *architecture* for N apps is done and genuinely good:

- `shared/store.js` — one DB, `allFiles(prefix)` already takes a prefix, kv keys already namespaced (`mine.*`, `calendar.*`).
- `shared/github.js` — the queue, the drain, the conflict rules and the sync record are app-agnostic. A diary gets atomic commits and conflict handling for free.
- `shared/md.js` / `markdown.js` / `prefs.js` — already correctly factored (envelope vs. renderer vs. Mine-wide prefs).
- `shared/apps.js` + `sw.js` + the tile screen — adding an app is one array entry, and `addAll` failing loudly on a bad path is the right trade.
- Topology: one manifest scope, same-origin storage, CSP. Verified on device.

So this is not a re-architecture. It's about four concrete things that would become copy-paste.

## 1. Shared code with non-shared CSS (the real bug)

`shared/markdown.js` is advertised in REQUIREMENTS.md as "one renderer, used by all of them" — but every `.md-*` rule lives in `calendar/style.css:615-630`. A diary importing the shared renderer renders **unstyled**. Root `style.css` has zero `md-` rules.

Same shape, one layer up: `calendar/style.css:7` carries `[hidden] { display: none !important }` with a comment explaining the trap (an id/class `display` rule beats the UA `[hidden]`). Every new app hits that trap once.

Move both into the shared base.

## 2. Root `style.css` is two things at once

It's the shared base *and* the home screen's stylesheet. The home-screen rules are hostile to app pages:

```
body   { max-width: 44rem; padding: 16px … }
button { width: 100%; padding: .9rem }
input  { display: block; width: 100% }
label  { display: block }
```

The calendar already undoes them (`body { max-width: none; padding: 0 }`) and re-declares its own `.nav` / `.ib` / `.srow` from scratch. Every app would repeat that.

Split: `style.css` keeps tokens + `*`/`body` basics + `.bad` + `[hidden]` + `.md-*`; the tile/setup/verify rules move to a new `home.css` that only root `index.html` loads. One caveat — `.link` is coloured `var(--today)`, which is calendar vocabulary; the shared base needs its own `--link` token (light + dark + `[data-theme]`).

## 3. `appName()` is hardcoded

`shared/github.js:63`:

```js
const appName = () => globalThis.location?.pathname.includes('/calendar/') ? 'calendar' : 'mine';
```

Every diary push would be recorded as coming "from mine". Derive the slug from the path generically (and keep the `globalThis.location?.` guard — `unit.mjs` imports this path in node).

## 4. The sync line and the logs panel are generic but live in `calendar/`

This is the biggest duplication, ~190 lines that a second app needs *verbatim*:

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| `calendar/app.js:289-355` | `status`, the `chain`/`serial` single-flight, `push`, `attempt`, `refresh` (drain-then-pull, focus retry) |
| `calendar/settings.js:249-328` | `renderLogs`, `actions` (push now / discard all), `headline`, `stamp`, `seen`, `age` |
| `calendar/index.html` | the `#sync` button and the `#logs-panel` block |
| `calendar/style.css:571-592` | `.lhead .lline .lnote .lrow .lop .lpath .lage` |

None of it knows anything about calendars. It reads `queued()`, `lastSync()`, `discardQueue()`, `drain()`, `pull()` and calls back for "the model changed, redraw".

Also generic, and also stuck in `calendar/`:

- `calendar/ui.js:12-19` — `$`, `el`, `phone` (trivial, but still three copies).
- `calendar/ui.js:90-160` — the `ICON` table and `icon()` / `iconBtn()`. Most of it is generic (`x plus trash disk pen gear menu logs filter chev check lines house zoom ball person bell`); only `cal board cols glass repeat` are calendar words.
- `calendar/ui.js:163-195` — `openCentred` / `place` / `openPop` / `openRowPop` / `closePops`, plus `.ib .pop .pop-head .scrim .centred .panel .modal .card .link .ask` CSS. The one blocker: `POPS` at line 190 is a hardcoded list of calendar ids.
- `calendar/settings.js:133-195` — `row`, `choose`, `toggle`, `numberField`, `dateField`. REQUIREMENTS.md *requires* the theme and date-format rows in every app's settings, so every app needs this kit.

## 5. One latent trap worth closing

`pull(prefix)` filters the tree by prefix but stores the **single shared** `commitEtag` regardless (`shared/github.js:108-121`). So a diary that reasonably wrote `pull('diary/')` would set the repo-wide ETag after mirroring only its own folder, and the calendar's next `pull()` would 304 forever and never fetch its files. Both callers pass no prefix today, so it's latent — but it's exactly the parameter a new app author reaches for. I'd delete the parameter (it's unused and unsafe); flagging rather than doing it since it's pre-existing.

## Recommended plan

**Phase A — moves only, no new concepts** (safe, do first)

1. `.md-*` and `[hidden]` → root `style.css`; add a `--link` token.
2. Home-only rules → new `home.css`, loaded only by root `index.html`; drop the calendar's `body` undo.
3. Fix `appName()`.
4. Move the generic chrome CSS (`.ib .pop .scrim .centred .panel .modal .card .link .srow .slab .sval .l* .ask`) from `calendar/style.css` into the shared base. `calendar/style.css` keeps the views, the top pane, the picker, the kanban, the entry popup, the group manager.

**Phase B — two new modules, nothing invented** (do before writing the diary)

5. `shared/ui.js` — `$`, `el`, `phone`, the generic icons, `icon`/`iconBtn`, the overlay helpers, and the settings-row kit. `closePops` takes its list from a registry the app fills at boot instead of a literal. `calendar/ui.js` keeps `S`, the calendar icons (merged on top), `colorOf`/`labelOf`/`viewRange`/`weekLetters`/`inkOn`.
6. `shared/sync.js` — the status line + single-flight push/refresh + the logs panel, as a factory taking "redraw the model" and the Mine-wide settings rows. `calendar/app.js` loses ~50 lines, `calendar/settings.js` loses ~80.

The rule for both: move what the calendar already does, verbatim. No options, no hooks, no "configurability" for a second caller that doesn't exist yet.

**Phase C — tests** (same commit as B, or the diary lands untested)

7. `test/check.mjs` is 1828 lines and 100% calendar. Split the CDP plumbing (lines 1-110) into `test/cdp.mjs`, the body into `test/calendar.mjs`, and let `run.sh` loop over `test/<app>.mjs`. Add `test/chrome.mjs` for what Phase B made shared (overlays, logs panel, markdown rendering in both schemes).
8. `serve.py`'s `/__fixture.json` → `/__fixture/<app>.json` dispatching per app. `unit.mjs` can stay one file until a second app has pure logic worth checking.

**Phase D — docs** (cheap, and this repo's docs are its design record)

9. Root `TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md`: update the Layout block, and add a short "adding an app" checklist — folder, `icon.svg`, the `index.html` head boilerplate (CSP, both stylesheets, theme-color), the `APPS` entry with its `files`, bump `sw.js` `VERSION`, the `REQUIREMENTS.md`/`TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md` pair and `sample/`.

## What I would *not* do

- **Don't abstract the `needs-setup` gate or the boot preamble.** It's six lines of HTML and one `if`. Copying it is cheaper than a shell abstraction.
- **Don't abstract the discard-prompt JS.** Its CSS moves with the rest of the chrome; `popup.js`'s ask flow stays calendar-local until the diary actually needs one.
- **Don't build the tile-screen per-app summary hook yet.** REQUIREMENTS.md promises it and it isn't built. The natural shape is an optional `summary` flag in `APPS` plus a dynamic `import('./<slug>/summary.js')` from the root app — but designing that contract against one app is guessing. Build it when the diary gives you a second real summary.
- **Don't generalise `calendar/data.js` or `popup.js`.** The model (occurrences, rrule, sprints, zones) and the entry popup's field machinery are genuinely calendar-specific. A diary's model is ~30 lines of its own.
- **Don't add a build step or a manifest generator** for the `APPS.files` list. It's hand-written on purpose and `addAll` fails loudly; that reasoning is already documented and still holds.

Phases A and B together are roughly a 400-line move plus two small decouplings (`POPS` → registry, sync → factory), and no behaviour change — which means the existing suite should pass unmodified, so you'll know if a move went wrong. Want me to start on A?
Start with A. If finished commit. Then continue with B. If finished commit. Then push and I will check on my laptop/android. If everythings works I will provide further instructions.
